title: Source systems and file formats
summary: Operational and analytical systems lay data out differently; file formats, Parquet internals, compression and schema evolution follow from that difference.

blocks.text: 3.1 OLTP versus OLAP

**OLTP** (online transaction processing) systems run the business: order entry, payments, user accounts. They handle many small reads and writes touching a few rows each, need millisecond latency and strong consistency, and are normalized (Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle). **OLAP** (online analytical processing) systems answer questions across the business: they scan millions or billions of rows, read a few columns, aggregate and join, and are mostly append-only.

head: Property
OLTP
OLAP
rows: Fetch or update one order by id
Revenue by month and region over 3 years

blocks.text: Running analytical queries directly on the production OLTP database is a classic anti-pattern: long scans compete with customer transactions. Use a read replica at minimum, ideally CDC (chapter 17).
3.2 Row versus columnar layout

A row layout stores all values of one record together. Reading a full record is one contiguous read, which suits OLTP. A columnar layout stores all values of one column together. A query that needs 3 of 80 columns reads roughly 3/80 of the data, and because a column holds values of one type that are often similar, it compresses far better.

blocks.title: The same three rows in two layouts
blocks.text:
Rows: (1, 'DE', 20.0)  (2, 'FR', 35.5)  (3, 'DE', 12.0)

Row layout:      [1|DE|20.0] [2|FR|35.5] [3|DE|12.0]

Columnar layout: id:      [1 | 2 | 3]
                 country: [DE | FR | DE]   -> dictionary {DE:0, FR:1}
                 amount:  [20.0 | 35.5 | 12.0]

Columnar layouts also enable **vectorized execution**: tight loops over batches of one column's values, which suit CPU caches and SIMD. The cost is on writes: inserting one row touches every column, so columnar formats are written in large batches and are effectively immutable once written.

rows: External `.proto`; field numbers on the wire

blocks.text: A good rule: **row formats for data in motion, columnar formats for data at rest**. Avro or Protobuf suit messages; Parquet or ORC suit analytical tables. CSV and JSON are interchange formats; convert them to Parquet early.
A single gzip-compressed CSV or JSON file cannot be split: one task must decompress it from the start. A 20 GB `.csv.gz` file therefore processes on one core no matter how big the cluster is.
3.4 Inside a Parquet file

blocks.title: Parquet file structure

layers.label: File
layers.sub: magic bytes PAR1 at start and end

layers.label: Row groups
layers.sub: horizontal slices, commonly 64 MB-1 GB uncompressed

layers.label: Column chunks
layers.sub: one per column per row group, with min/max/null-count statistics

layers.label: Pages
layers.sub: unit of encoding and compression, commonly around 1 MB

layers.label: Footer
layers.sub: schema, row group offsets, column statistics

blocks.caption: Readers read the footer first, then fetch only the column chunks and row groups they need.

items: **Projection pushdown**: only the column chunks for requested columns are read.

**Predicate pushdown**: row group statistics (min, max, null count) let a reader skip row groups that cannot match `WHERE order_date = '2026-01-15'`. Optional page indexes and bloom filters allow finer skipping.
**Dictionary encoding**: low-cardinality columns store a dictionary plus small integer indexes. Writers fall back to plain encoding when the dictionary grows too large.
**RLE and bit-packing**: runs of repeated values and small integers are stored compactly; also used for dictionary indexes and for the definition and repetition levels that encode nulls and nesting.
**Delta encodings**: store differences between consecutive values, effective for sorted ids and timestamps.

blocks.text: Statistics only help if values are clustered. If `customer_id` is randomly distributed, every row group spans almost the full range and nothing is skipped. Sorting or clustering data on common filter columns before writing (chapter 25 covers this for Iceberg) can turn a full scan into reading a few percent of the file.

blocks.title: Write Parquet and inspect row group statistics with PyArrow
blocks.text:
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

table = pa.table({
    "order_id": list(range(1_000_000)),
    "country": ["DE", "FR", "NL", "ES"] * 250_000,
})

# row_group_size is a number of rows, not bytes
pq.write_table(table, "orders.parquet",
               compression="zstd", row_group_size=250_000)

meta = pq.ParquetFile("orders.parquet").metadata
print(meta.num_row_groups)                      # 4
stats = meta.row_group(1).column(0).statistics
print(stats.min, stats.max)                     # 250000 499999
ORC is similar: **stripes** play the role of row groups, with lightweight row indexes and optional bloom filters. Parquet has broader engine support today.
3.5 Compression codecs

Columnar formats compress each page with a general-purpose codec after encoding, trading CPU time against size and I/O. Encoding does most of the work on repetitive columns, so layout matters more than the codec.

head: Codec
Ratio
Speed
Notes
rows: Long-time default in Spark and many tools
Common modern default; usually smaller than Snappy at similar speed
Rarely right for object storage, where I/O dominates

blocks.text: 3.6 Schema evolution per format
Columns get added, renamed, widened or dropped; each format decides how much of that breaks downstream.

head: Format
Add field
Rename / remove
Mechanism
rows: Safe if the new field has a default
Aliases support renames; removal needs a default
Reader schema resolved against writer schema
Safe with a new field number
Never reuse a number; mark it reserved
Field numbers, not names, on the wire
Safe; old files read as null
Each file carries its own schema

blocks.text: Plain Parquet directories match columns by name (or position), so a rename looks like a dropped column plus a new empty one. Table formats such as Iceberg solve this by assigning stable **field IDs** to columns, decoupling the logical name from the physical column; see chapter 23. For messages, a **schema registry** enforces compatibility rules (backward, forward, full) before a producer can publish a breaking change; see chapter 18.

blocks.title: Landing CDC events
blocks.text: A team lands Debezium change events from Postgres into the lake. Events travel through Kafka as Avro with a schema registry enforcing backward compatibility.
items: A new nullable column produces a new Avro schema version with a null default; consumers keep working.
Downstream tables are kept in Iceberg so later renames are metadata-only.
`int` to `bigint` is allowed; `varchar` to `int` is blocked and raised with the source team.

blocks.title: Pick formats for three flows
blocks.text: Choose a format and codec for: (a) a partner who sends a daily 5 GB product catalogue, (b) clickstream events published by 40 microservices, (c) a 3 TB fact table queried mostly by date and country. For each, explain how schema changes will be handled and what will be split or skipped at read time.
hints: Consider who controls the schema in each flow.
For (c), think about sort order and row group statistics.

items: OLTP is row-oriented for small transactions; OLAP is columnar for large scans of few columns.
Row formats (Avro, Protobuf) suit data in motion; columnar formats (Parquet, ORC) suit data at rest.
Parquet is organized as row groups, column chunks and pages, with footer statistics enabling projection and predicate pushdown.
Statistics skip data only when values are clustered; sort on common filter columns.
Schema evolution differs by format: Avro uses defaults, Protobuf uses field numbers, Parquet matches by name, Iceberg adds field IDs.

blocks.q: A query reads 4 of 120 columns from a large table. Why is Parquet much faster than CSV here?
options: CSV cannot be read in parallel under any circumstances
Parquet keeps all data in memory
Only the column chunks for the 4 columns are read, and they are compressed
blocks.explain: Projection pushdown reads only the needed columns, which are also well compressed. CSV can be split when uncompressed, and Parquet is not sorted unless the writer sorted it.

blocks.q: A filter `WHERE customer_id = 42` scans every row group of a Parquet file. What is the most likely cause?
options: Customer ids are spread randomly, so every row group's min/max range includes 42
The file uses ZSTD instead of Snappy
blocks.explain: Min/max statistics only skip row groups when the value falls outside their range. Unclustered data gives every row group a wide range. The codec and encoding do not disable statistics.

blocks.q: In Protobuf, what is the safe way to stop using a field?
options: Rename it and keep the number
Delete it and mark its number (and name) as reserved
Reuse its field number for the replacement field
blocks.explain: Reserving prevents the number from being reused, which would make old messages decode into the wrong field. Reusing a number is the classic Protobuf compatibility bug.

blocks.q: Why does a 20 GB `.csv.gz` file process slowly on a large Spark cluster?
options: Gzip streams are not splittable, so one task must read the file sequentially
Compression ratio of gzip is poor
blocks.explain: A single gzip stream can only be decompressed from the start, so parallelism is one task. Spark reads gzip fine; the lack of schema slows inference but does not serialize the read.
